subject: Mining
practicalPaper: There is no separate practical paper: Papers 1 and 2 are written, but field work forms 40 percent of the continuous assessment scores sent to WAEC. Practical skills — identifying minerals and rocks, reading geological and mineral maps, drawing cross-sections, sampling, processing calculations and mine safety — are examined through structured and essay questions.

practicals.title: Mapping the distribution of minerals in Nigeria
practicals.aim: To prepare a map showing the locations of major solid minerals in Nigeria and classify the minerals.
apparatus: Outline map of Nigeria with states
materials: Mineral samples or pictures (cassiterite, coal, limestone, iron ore, gold, lead-zinc ore, bitumen, gypsum, barite)
safety: Handle mineral samples with clean hands; wash hands after handling lead ores.
procedure: Classify minerals as metallic, non-metallic and energy (fuel) minerals.
Using the reference map, mark each mineral with a symbol on the outline map.
Use a key with symbols and colours.
Add a title, north point and scale.
Write one economic use of each mineral.
practicals.expectedObservations: Examples: tin (cassiterite) and columbite – Jos Plateau; coal – Enugu and Kogi; iron ore – Itakpe (Kogi); limestone – Ogun, Cross River, Benue; lead-zinc – Ebonyi, Nasarawa; gold – Zamfara, Osun, Niger; bitumen – Ondo; barite – Benue trough.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Map scale: on a map at 1:5 000 000, Jos to Enugu measures 7.6 cm → 7.6 × 5 000 000 cm = 38 000 000 cm = 380 km straight-line distance.
precautions: Place symbols accurately in the correct state.
commonMistakes: Mixing up states for coal (Enugu) and iron ore (Itakpe, Kogi).
examTips: Give examples for each class of mineral with locations.
State the importance of minerals to the economy.

practicals.title: Identifying rock-forming minerals by physical properties
practicals.aim: To identify common rock-forming and ore minerals using colour, lustre, streak, hardness, cleavage and specific gravity.
apparatus: Spring balance or electronic balance with beaker of water
materials: Samples: quartz, feldspar, mica, calcite, hematite, magnetite, galena, cassiterite
safety: Wear goggles when using dilute acid; teacher dispenses it.
Wash hands after handling galena (lead mineral).
procedure: Record colour and lustre (metallic or non-metallic).
Rub on the streak plate and record streak colour.
Test hardness with fingernail (2.5), copper coin (3.5), glass (5.5) and steel knife (about 5.5–6.5) against the Mohs scale.
Observe cleavage or fracture with the hand lens.
Test with a magnet and dilute acid.
Determine specific gravity by weighing in air and in water.
Identify each mineral using a table.
practicals.expectedObservations: Quartz scratches glass and has no cleavage; calcite fizzes in acid and has rhombic cleavage; hematite gives a red-brown streak; magnetite is magnetic with a black streak; galena is heavy with cubic cleavage.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Specific gravity = weight in air/(weight in air − weight in water). Sample: 26.5 g in air, 16.5 g in water → SG = 26.5/(26.5 − 16.5) = 2.65 (quartz). Galena gives about 7.5.
precautions: Remove air bubbles when weighing in water.
commonMistakes: Confusing streak colour with body colour.
examTips: List Mohs scale minerals 1–10 (talc to diamond).
Show the SG formula and working.

practicals.title: Identifying igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
practicals.aim: To classify rock samples into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic types using texture and mineral content, and relate them to the rock cycle.
materials: Granite, basalt, sandstone, shale, limestone, conglomerate, marble, gneiss, schist, quartzite samples
safety: Goggles for acid tests; handle sharp rock edges with care.
procedure: Examine grain size and texture (crystalline, clastic, foliated).
Identify visible minerals.
Test for carbonate with acid.
Classify each rock and name it.
State the origin of each type.
Draw the rock cycle showing how each type forms from the others.
practicals.expectedObservations: Granite has large interlocking crystals (intrusive igneous); basalt is fine-grained (extrusive); sandstone has rounded grains (sedimentary); gneiss shows banding (metamorphic); marble fizzes and is crystalline.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Grain-size scale: coarse > 2 mm, medium 0.06–2 mm, fine < 0.06 mm. A granite with feldspar crystals 5 mm across is coarse-grained, showing slow cooling at depth.
examTips: Give Nigerian examples: Basement Complex granites and gneisses; sedimentary basins (Benue trough, Niger Delta).
Explain the rock cycle and weathering.

practicals.title: Reading geological maps and drawing a cross-section
practicals.aim: To interpret a simplified geological map and draw a geological cross-section along a given line.
materials: Simplified geological map with contours and rock boundaries
safety: Normal classroom safety.
procedure: Read the key: rock units, dip symbols, faults.
Draw line X–Y on the map.
Lay paper edge along X–Y and mark contour crossings and rock boundaries.
Construct the topographic profile on graph paper with a chosen vertical scale.
Transfer boundaries onto the profile and draw beds using their dip.
Shade and label units; state the vertical exaggeration.
Describe the geological history.
practicals.expectedObservations: The section shows how rock layers lie below the surface, their dips and any faults or intrusions.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Horizontal scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m); vertical scale 1 cm = 100 m. Vertical exaggeration = 500/100 = 5. A bed with outcrop width 20 m on flat ground dipping 30° has true thickness = 20 × sin 30° = 10 m.
commonMistakes: Drawing beds horizontal when the map shows dip.
examTips: Neat, labelled sections with title, scales and key earn marks.
Interpret topographical and geological maps together.

practicals.title: Field excursion: measuring strike and dip and collecting geological data
practicals.aim: To collect and collate geological data from an outcrop: rock type, strike, dip, structures and samples.
safety: Wear helmet, goggles and boots; never hammer near others or at loose faces.
Get permission to enter land; work in groups with a teacher.
Carry water and a first aid kit.
procedure: Locate the outcrop on the map and record GPS coordinates.
Describe rock type, colour, texture and structures (joints, folds, veins).
Measure strike with the compass and dip with the clinometer on a bedding or foliation plane.
Sketch the outcrop with a scale.
Collect labelled samples.
Collate data in a table and plot on the map.
practicals.expectedObservations: Consistent strike and dip readings across nearby outcrops show the regional structure; veins may carry mineralisation.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Readings of dip at one outcrop: 32°, 35°, 33°, 36° → mean = (32 + 35 + 33 + 36)/4 = 34°. Record strike/dip as e.g. 045°/34° SE.
precautions: Keep the compass away from the hammer and phone.
sourcesOfError: Measuring on joints instead of bedding.
examTips: Field work counts for continuous assessment — keep a neat notebook.
Define strike and dip.

practicals.title: Stream sediment sampling and panning for heavy minerals
practicals.topic: Stages of Development in Mining (Basic Concepts)
practicals.aim: To collect stream sediment samples and concentrate heavy minerals by panning as a simple prospecting technique.
safety: Work only in shallow, slow water with a partner; avoid streams after heavy rain.
Wear boots and gloves; beware of snakes and sharp objects.
procedure: Choose sites where heavy minerals collect (inside bends, behind boulders).
Collect a measured volume or mass of sediment; record location.
Sieve to remove coarse gravel.
Pan: swirl under water so light material washes out and heavy grains settle.
Examine the concentrate with the hand lens; remove magnetite with the magnet.
Weigh the concentrate; estimate the grade.
Plot results to find where the mineral comes from.
practicals.expectedObservations: A black sand concentrate remains (magnetite, ilmenite, cassiterite); gold, if present, shows as bright yellow specks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: 20 kg (0.02 t) of gravel yields 0.06 g of gold → grade = 0.06/0.02 = 3 g/t. Samples upstream with higher grades point to the source.
precautions: Pan the same mass at each site for fair comparison.
commonMistakes: Sampling the wrong part of the stream.
examTips: Name prospecting techniques: geological, geophysical, geochemical, remote sensing.
Distinguish prospecting and exploration.

practicals.title: Quarry visit: unit operations and flow sheet
practicals.aim: To observe quarry operations and draw a flow sheet from drilling and blasting to stockpiling of crushed aggregate.
safety: Wear helmet, hi-vis vest, boots, ear defenders and dust mask provided by the quarry.
Stay with the guide; obey blast warning signals and keep out of vehicle routes.
procedure: Attend the safety induction.
Observe and record unit operations: drilling, blasting, loading, hauling, crushing (primary/secondary), screening, stockpiling.
Note equipment used at each stage.
Record bench height and blast pattern from the guide.
Note environmental controls (dust suppression, noise).
Draw the flow sheet and write a report.
practicals.expectedObservations: Rock moves from the blasted face to the crusher by loaders and trucks, is crushed and screened into sizes (e.g. 3/4 in, 1/2 in, dust) and stockpiled.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Blast hole pattern: burden 3.0 m × spacing 3.5 m × bench height 10 m = 105 m³ of rock per hole. At density 2.7 t/m³: 105 × 2.7 = 283.5 t per hole.
precautions: Never enter areas without the guide.
sourcesOfError: Production figures quoted vary by day.
commonMistakes: Wrong order of operations in the flow sheet.
examTips: Define quarrying and its products (aggregate, dimension stone).
Draw a neat flow sheet with arrows.

practicals.title: Room-and-pillar mine model and extraction ratio
practicals.aim: To build or draw a model of a room-and-pillar mine, identify underground features and calculate the extraction ratio.
materials: Cardboard, foam or clay for the model
safety: Use cutting tools carefully under supervision.
procedure: Draw a plan of a flat seam with square pillars and rooms on graph paper.
Build the model showing shaft or adit, main roadways, rooms and pillars.
Label features: shaft, adit, drift, stope, crosscut, haulage way, ventilation route.
Calculate the extraction ratio for the layout.
Compare with longwall mining.
practicals.expectedObservations: Pillars left in place support the roof but lock up part of the ore; larger rooms raise extraction but reduce support.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Square pillars 12 m wide with 6 m rooms: centre-to-centre spacing = 18 m. Area per unit = 18² = 324 m²; pillar area = 12² = 144 m². Extraction ratio = 1 − 144/324 = 0.556 = 55.6%.
commonMistakes: Calculating the pillar fraction and calling it extraction.
examTips: Describe features of an underground mine and methods: room-and-pillar, longwall, cut-and-fill, shrinkage, block caving.
Compare surface and underground methods.

practicals.title: Truck haulage productivity
practicals.topic: Other Mining Methods and Materials Handling
practicals.aim: To identify materials handling equipment and calculate haulage productivity for trucks and conveyors.
apparatus: Pictures or videos of conveyor belts, dump trucks, pay-loaders
safety: On site, keep clear of moving equipment and blind spots.
procedure: Identify each item of materials handling equipment and its use.
Record truck capacity and cycle time (load, haul, dump, return).
Calculate hourly output per truck.
Work out the number of trucks needed for a target production.
Compare with a conveyor of given capacity.
practicals.expectedObservations: Trucks are flexible but costly per tonne over long distances; conveyors suit steady, long-distance transport.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Truck capacity 30 t, cycle time 20 min → trips per hour = 60/20 = 3; output = 3 × 30 = 90 t/h. For a target of 450 t/h, trucks needed = 450/90 = 5.
precautions: Use realistic cycle times including waiting.
examTips: Name equipment: conveyor belt, trucks, pay-loader, excavator, skip hoist.
Show productivity working.

practicals.title: Crushing and sieve analysis
practicals.aim: To reduce ore size by crushing, carry out a sieve analysis and calculate the reduction ratio.
apparatus: Jaw crusher or pestle and mortar
Set of sieves (e.g. 4.75, 2.36, 1.18, 0.6, 0.3 mm) with pan
materials: Ore or rock sample (e.g. 1 kg of 100 mm lumps)
safety: Wear goggles, gloves and dust mask; keep fingers out of the crusher.
procedure: Measure the top feed size.
Crush the sample.
Weigh the crushed product.
Shake through the sieve stack for 10 minutes.
Weigh material retained on each sieve.
Calculate % retained and cumulative % passing; plot a size distribution graph.
Read the size at which 80% passes (P80) and calculate the reduction ratio.
practicals.expectedObservations: Most material passes the coarser sieves; a smooth cumulative curve is obtained.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Feed F80 = 100 mm; product P80 = 20 mm → reduction ratio = 100/20 = 5. Sieve check: 1 000 g sample, 180 g retained on 4.75 mm → 18% retained; cumulative passing = 82%.
commonMistakes: Plotting % retained instead of cumulative % passing.
examTips: Define comminution, crushing, grinding, liberation.
Show the reduction ratio calculation.

practicals.title: Gravity and magnetic concentration with recovery calculation
practicals.aim: To concentrate a heavy mineral by gravity (panning/shaking) and magnetite by a magnet, and calculate grade, recovery and ratio of concentration.
materials: Synthetic ore: 2 kg sand mixed with 100 g of heavy mineral (e.g. magnetite or ilmenite sand)
safety: Keep the work area tidy and dry around balances.
procedure: Weigh the feed and note its grade.
Separate by panning or sluicing into concentrate and tailings.
Run a magnet (in a bag) through the concentrate to pull out magnetite.
Dry and weigh concentrate and tailings.
Estimate the grade of the concentrate (by magnet separation of a subsample).
Calculate recovery and ratio of concentration.
practicals.expectedObservations: A small mass of dark, heavy concentrate is obtained; tailings are mostly light quartz sand.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Feed 2 000 g at 5% → 100 g valuable mineral. Concentrate 150 g at 60% → 0.6 × 150 = 90 g mineral. Recovery = 90/100 × 100 = 90%. Ratio of concentration = 2 000/150 = 13.3.
sourcesOfError: Fine particles lost in wash water.
commonMistakes: Confusing grade (% in concentrate) with recovery (% of mineral recovered).
examTips: Define concentrate, tailings, middlings, grade, recovery.
State properties used: specific gravity, magnetism, surface properties.

practicals.title: Identifying gemstones and calculating carat weight
practicals.aim: To identify gemstones by colour, lustre, hardness, specific gravity and refractive index, and express weight in carats.
materials: Rough and cut samples: tourmaline, aquamarine (beryl), topaz, garnet, amethyst (quartz), sapphire; glass imitation
safety: Handle stones over a padded tray; refractometer contact liquid is toxic — teacher only.
procedure: Observe colour, transparency and lustre with the loupe.
Look for inclusions (natural) versus bubbles (glass).
Weigh in carats and determine SG by hydrostatic weighing.
Measure refractive index if a refractometer is available.
Identify each stone with a table.
Describe faceting and polishing machines used in lapidary.
practicals.expectedObservations: Natural stones often have inclusions; glass may show round gas bubbles and lower hardness. Tourmaline and beryl are notable Nigerian gemstones (e.g. Oyo, Nasarawa, Plateau).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: 1 carat = 0.2 g. A stone of 3.5 g = 3.5/0.2 = 17.5 ct. SG: 3.50 g in air, 2.40 g in water → 3.50/1.10 = 3.18 (consistent with tourmaline ≈ 3.0–3.3).
precautions: Use tweezers to avoid finger grease.
examTips: Name gem properties: hardness, RI, SG, colour, clarity, cut.
Explain factors that affect price (the four Cs).

practicals.title: Mine safety: PPE, first aid and accident reporting
practicals.aim: To identify mining PPE and safety equipment, administer simple first aid and complete an accident report.
safety: Practise first aid only on volunteers with no real injuries; do not give drugs without training and authority.
procedure: Identify each item of PPE and the hazard it controls (falling rock, dust, noise, gases).
Demonstrate the primary survey (danger, response, airway, breathing, circulation).
Dress a wound and splint a suspected fracture.
Complete an accident report: date, time, place, persons, description, injuries, action, witnesses.
List diseases associated with mining (silicosis, lead poisoning, hearing loss, malaria in camps).
Discuss reporting procedures to the mine manager and Mines Inspectorate.
practicals.expectedObservations: Students wear PPE correctly, perform first aid in order and fill the accident form completely.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Lost-time injury frequency rate = injuries × 1 000 000/hours worked. 3 lost-time injuries in 600 000 hours → 3 × 1 000 000/600 000 = 5.0 per million hours.
precautions: Ensure scene safety before giving first aid.
commonMistakes: Moving a casualty with suspected spinal injury.
examTips: List health hazards, safety measures and PPE in tables.
Mention the Nigerian Minerals and Mining Act and environmental laws.

practicals.title: Assessing the environmental impact of a mine site
practicals.aim: To observe and record the environmental effects of a mining or quarrying site and propose control measures.
safety: Visit only with permission and a guide; avoid open pits, ponds and unstable spoil heaps.
Do not drink or touch untested water.
procedure: Record land disturbance: pits, spoil heaps, vegetation loss, erosion.
Observe water: colour, turbidity, test pH upstream and downstream.
Note dust and noise sources and nearby communities.
Record any reclamation (backfilling, tree planting).
Estimate disturbed area.
Write a report with control measures.
practicals.expectedObservations: Abandoned pits, silted streams, bare land and dust are common impacts; reclaimed areas show regrowth.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Disturbed area: pit 120 m × 80 m = 9 600 m² = 0.96 ha. If reclamation costs ₦2 500 000 per hectare, cost ≈ 0.96 × 2 500 000 = ₦2 400 000. pH upstream 6.8, downstream 4.9 → water downstream is more acidic.
precautions: Take water samples at the same depth and time.
sourcesOfError: Single-visit observations may not represent all seasons.
examTips: Describe impacts (land, water, air, social) and steps for environmental control.
Refer to the National Policy on the Environment and EIA requirements.
